overview: The Medford School Committee is the governing body for the Medford Public Schools district, responsible for policy adoption, operational budgeting, collective bargaining, and capital facilities planning. The archive holds 82 meetings spanning from February 12, 2024, through October 5, 2026. Across this period, the committee resolved executive leadership by appointing and contracting a permanent superintendent, approved consecutive operating budgets and major school HVAC capital bond authorizations, and advanced the comprehensive high school building project through state feasibility milestones. At its most recent meeting, the committee deliberated a proposed elementary school reassignment policy, reviewed student transit data on a new high school late bus, and received survey findings for an ongoing district strategic plan.

threads.name: Medford High School MSBA building project
threads.summary: The committee established the Medford Comprehensive High School Building Committee, confirmed project educational goals, and designated leadership and governance structures under Massachusetts School Building Authority guidelines (M01#5, M02#7). Following enrollment certification at 1,395 students, the body approved the MSBA feasibility study agreement and engaged Left Field as Owner's Project Manager (M38#7, M39#4, M46#5). After discovering a 1967 state deed restriction on Edgley Field, the committee eliminated conflicting site configurations and selected modified alternatives for the Preferred Schematic Report (M71#2, M74#3). Work continued with approvals for educational plan revisions, space consolidation, Chapter 74 viability documentation, and LEED v4 Silver sustainability objectives (M76#7, M77#1, M78#7, M79#9).

threads.name: Superintendent leadership and evaluation
threads.summary: The committee conducted strategy sessions regarding the contract of Superintendent Dr. Marice Edouard-Vincent before announcing her departure in early 2025 after a seven-year tenure (M17#2, M34#3, M35#5). Assistant Superintendent Dr. Suzanne Galusi was appointed Interim Superintendent, approved for an interim contract, and granted a conflict of interest clearance for collective bargaining (M33#2, M35#3, M37#1). The committee subsequently conducted formal goal-setting reviews, monitored transition entry findings, and gathered public survey data on district leadership expectations (M54#13, M57#5, M62#6, M62#10). In February 2026, the committee voted to appoint Dr. Galusi as permanent superintendent and later finalized a three-year employment agreement realigned with the academic calendar (M63#4, M69#6, M76#11, M80#6).

threads.name: District operating budget and capital infrastructure
threads.summary: After addressing a projected mid-year deficit of $2.5 million in fiscal year 2024 through encumbrance adjustments and deferred spending, the committee adopted a $77.75 million FY25 budget and passed supplemental appropriations funded by municipal override ballot questions (M01#4, M04#5, M15#7, M35#7). The committee pursued large-scale facility upgrades, authorizing a $25.77 million bond to overhaul HVAC systems at the McGlynn and Andrews schools and commissioning a district-wide facility condition assessment (M09#6, M34#6, M43#7, M57#3). In FY27 budget cycles, the committee worked with municipal officials on an initial $5 million level-service deficit, established a special education reserve fund, and approved a $22.7 million schematic design for Roberts Elementary HVAC and roof replacements (M67#3, M75#10, M76#4, M79#4). The committee also approved power purchase agreements for solar installations and reallocated capital balances for school equipment maintenance (M59#4, M79#5, M81#4).

threads.name: Elementary capacity and grade reconfiguration
threads.summary: Severe enrollment imbalances and facility crowding at Roberts Elementary School prompted requests from school staff for redistricting and long-term space planning (M20#8, M21#6). The committee responded in the short term by transferring preschool classrooms to Missituk Elementary, adding staff, and authorizing an architectural space utilization study (M44#4, M49#6, M49#7). When consultants presented grade reconfiguration models that would shift middle schools to grades 5-8, the committee solicited community input and ultimately voted to postpone implementation to no earlier than the 2028-2029 school year (M58#5, M59#5, M78#4). Most recently, the committee took up a draft intra-district reassignment policy to standardize criteria and enrollment buffers for student transfers (M54#11, M82#5).

threads.name: Student transportation and route operations
threads.summary: Persistent regional bus driver shortages by contractor Eastern Bus created overcrowding, delayed routes, and forced policy evaluations around walking distances and MBTA alternatives (M06#1, M20#12, M26#4). The committee approved a successor five-year contract with Eastern Bus, directed the exploration of bus electrification, and supported municipal adoption of automated stop-arm camera enforcement (M50#4, M53#8). To address bus safety and behavioral concerns, the administration established a tiered system deploying paraprofessionals as rotating monitors and hired a transportation manager (M54#9, M55#5, M56#6). Student representatives later presented operational updates on high school boarding infrastructure and the rollout of an extracurricular late bus service (M58#3, M82#4).

threads.name: Before- and after-school programming expansion
threads.summary: Faced with lengthy registration waitlists and rising program costs, the committee regularly adjusted fee rate cards for after-school care, Kids' Corner, and summer programs (M03#7, M25#8, M38#4, M44#1, M45#5). The district integrated City Year AmeriCorps members into schools, elevated site coordinators to full-time status, and engaged the Belmont After School Enrichment Collaborative to design an operational overhaul (M15#4, M47#2, M52#3, M69#4). Based on consultant findings, the committee adopted a restructured model introducing full-time site directors, added 150 student seats, created a flexible 4:00 p.m. pickup rate, and reduced waitlists by 68 percent (M50#5, M69#4, M69#5, M80#5).

threads.name: Career and Technical Education policy and access
threads.summary: The committee coordinated with vocational leadership to align Chapter 74 program offerings with the high school MSBA feasibility study, adding new programs while dropping others to manage space (M11#8, M30#4, M40#6). To eliminate discriminatory barriers and meet state guidance, the committee repealed selective admissions criteria and adopted a non-weighted lottery policy for oversubscribed vocational technical programs (M55#3, M56#4, M68#3). The committee approved an updated Chapter 74 viability submission detailing student demand and waitlists for the MSBA (M77#1). Academic pathways were further expanded by establishing an honors credit pilot for vocational upperclassmen engaged in cooperative education and capstone projects (M80#4).
